The SkyBridge founder reveals that crypto now represents about 60% of the firm’s assets, while Vlad explains why he keeps less than 1% in digital assets and favors cash-flowing businesses like Google stock.  

The conversation explores Bitcoin as “digital gold,” blockchain transparency, FBI and CIA perspectives on crypto scams, Mike Morell’s crypto analysis, and the risks of fraud compared with the U.S. dollar. Vlad counters with lessons from Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger, emphasizing compounding businesses over speculative stores of value. recentItems.title: Medellin Cartel Co-founder Carlos Lehder on Being Released from Prison After 33 Years (Part 12)
recentItems.description:
Become a VladStocks Member now: https://www.youtube.com/vladtv/join

Part 11: https://youtu.be/FmzR88KWLh8
Part 1: https://youtu.be/AxHbPY_r1q4
--------
Carlos Lehder, co-founder of the Medellín Cartel, reflects with Vlad on walking free in June 2020 at age 70 after more than 33 years in U.S. federal prison. Lehder says his release was approved by Attorney General William Barr during the Trump administration, noting Barr had also been connected to his earlier cooperation with U.S. authorities.

Now living in Germany, Lehder describes the shock of modern life—from smartphones to supermarkets—and the lingering “prisoner complex” after decades behind bars. He discusses rehabilitation, writing his book, and his message to younger generations about avoiding illegal narcotics, cocaine trafficking, and the drug trade. Lehder also shares his views on the DEA, FBI, Justice Department, global law enforcement technology, and controversial ideas for reducing drug consumption in America.

A rare firsthand account of prison, freedom, and life after the drug war.

--------
William Noguera sits down with Vlad to reflect on 42 years on death row and the moral weight of America’s death penalty. Speaking from his experience inside San Quentin, Noguera discusses whether innocent people end up condemned, why he believes capital punishment should be reserved only for the “worst of the worst,” and how wrongful convictions, false confessions, and police pressure complicate the debate.

The conversation also revisits the Central Park Five case as an example of young suspects being pushed into statements, while Vlad cites death row exoneration statistics and the execution of Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh. Noguera weighs the U.S. system against European countries that have abolished the death penalty, then reflects on prison culture, Cook County Jail stories involving Rico Recklezz, and his own exoneration from a special circumstance charge.

A candid discussion on justice, punishment, innocence, and life after death row.
